title: Anatomy of a function
summary: What a function is made of, how to read Excel’s tooltip, Insert Function, and functions inside functions.
objectives: Name the parts of a function: name, brackets, arguments and separators.
Tell required arguments from optional ones in Excel’s tooltip.
Build a function with Insert Function (Shift+F3) and the Function Arguments box.
Nest one function inside another and read it from the inside out.

slides.h: A function is a ready-made calculation
p: A **function** is a calculation Excel already knows. You hand it some values; it hands back one answer.
Excel has over 500 functions. About 40 cover most everyday work, and this course teaches them.
You already know five from C1: SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX and COUNT.
Change an input and the answer updates by itself.
In real life: doesn’t add 2,000 GST invoices by hand. One =SUM(F2:F2001) does it, and redoes it whenever an invoice changes.

terms: a value you hand to the function

items: SUM adds, ROUND rounds, IF decides

p: Every function is written the same way: **=NAME(argument1, argument2, …)**.
Arguments go inside the brackets, with a comma between each.
An argument can be a number, a cell, a range, text in "quotes", or another calculation.
A space after a comma is allowed but not needed.
In real life: prices every phone with 18% GST in whole rupees: =ROUND(B2*1.18,0) turns ₹13,499 into ₹15,929.

p: As you type a function, Excel shows a tooltip. The argument you’re on is **bold**; anything in [square brackets] is optional.
Leave out an optional argument and Excel uses its default value.
Click the function’s name in the tooltip to open its help page.
Type =ROUND then press **Ctrl+Shift+A** and Excel writes in every argument’s name as a reminder.
In real life: never memorises the order of arguments. She types the function, then reads the tooltip one bold word at a time.

check.q: In =ROUND(B2*1.18,0), what is the second argument?
check.explain: Arguments are separated by commas. B2*1.18 is the first; **0** (decimal places) is the second.

why.0: ROUND is the function’s name, not an argument.
why.1: That’s the first argument: the value to round.
why.3: 1.18 is part of the first argument.

slides.h: Insert Function: Excel fills in the form
p: Not sure which function, or what goes where? Click **fx** beside the formula bar (or press **Shift+F3**) and Excel walks you through it.
Search in plain words, such as “round a number” or “working days”.
Pick a function and click OK: the **Function Arguments** box opens.
It has one box per argument, says what each one means, and previews the answer.
In real life: typed “working days” into Insert Function’s search box and found NETWORKDAYS for the staff-leave sheet. She’d never heard of it.

p: Fill one box per argument. Excel shows each argument’s value on the right and the final answer at the bottom, before you click OK.
Click into a box, then click cells on the sheet to fill it.
Click **fx** again on an existing formula to reopen this box and check it.
Great for learning a new function’s arguments.
In real life: checks every new formula in Function Arguments first: if the preview looks wrong, he fixes it before anyone sees the report.

p: An argument can itself be a function. Excel works out the **inner one first**, then hands its answer to the outer one.
Read a nested formula from the inside out.
Every ( needs its ). While you type, Excel colours each bracket pair to help you match them.
Excel allows 64 levels; two or three keep a formula readable.
In real life: shows each batter’s average to one decimal with =ROUND(AVERAGE(C2:C11),1): AVERAGE runs first, then ROUND tidies it.

check.q: In =ROUND(SUM(A1:A3)/3,0), what does Excel work out first?
check.explain: The innermost part goes first: SUM(A1:A3). Then /3, then ROUND.

why.0: ROUND is the outer function: it runs last.
why.3: 0 is just a value; nothing to work out.

demo.intro: Price the print shop’s list with 18% GST in whole rupees, then nest AVERAGE inside ROUND.

steps.say: Start with the inner calculation: the price plus 18% GST.
411.82 isn’t a price anyone charges. Wrap it in ROUND, with 0 decimal places.
Fill it down: every price is rounded the same way.
…rounded to whole rupees: AVERAGE goes inside ROUND.
The fx? button shows how Excel works it out: the inner AVERAGE first, then ROUND.

demo.outro: Every function is a NAME with arguments in brackets, and nested ones work inside out.

13,499 × 1.18 = 15,928.82, and ROUND(…,0) gives the nearest whole number: 15,929.

quiz.q: In a function’s tooltip, what do [square brackets] around an argument mean?
quiz.explain: Bracketed arguments can be left out; Excel uses a default.
Shift+F3, or click fx beside the formula bar.

quiz.q: In what order does Excel work out =ROUND(AVERAGE(B2:B4),1)?
quiz.explain: Inner functions first: AVERAGE’s answer is handed to ROUND.
The first is missing its ), the second its brackets, and the last its = sign (Excel would show it as text).

points: A function is **=NAME(arguments)**: a ready-made calculation that gives one answer.
Arguments are separated by commas; ones in [brackets] are optional.
Nested functions work **inside out**. fx (Shift+F3) builds one for you.
